text: Aga Khan is the hereditary title of the imam of the Nizari Ismaili Muslims, a title first granted in the nineteenth century. The Nizari line traces its origins to the succession dispute of 1094 within the Fatimid Caliphate. It is cited in the Fatimid profile as a continuation of the Fatimid Ismaili tradition.

Alcuin of York was an English scholar and teacher who joined the court of Charlemagne in the late eighth century. He led the palace school and was a leader of the Carolingian Renaissance, promoting education, the copying of texts and reforms of script and liturgy. He later became abbot of St Martin's at Tours.

Alexander I of Russia was emperor of the Russian Empire from 1801 to 1825. He led Russia through the Napoleonic Wars, including the defeat of Napoleon's invasion in 1812, and Russian armies reached Paris in 1814. He took a central part in the Congress of Vienna, and his early reforming plans gave way to more conservative rule later in his reign.

The Amarna letters are a set of clay tablets from the 14th century BCE, discovered at Amarna in Egypt, recording diplomatic correspondence between Egyptian pharaohs and other rulers. Written mostly in Akkadian, the international language of the time, they include letters from the kings of Babylon, Mitanni, the Hittites and Levantine vassals. They show the role of the Egyptian New Kingdom in a network of great powers and the continuing influence of the Akkadian language.

Archery is the use of bows to shoot arrows in hunting and warfare. Mounted archers were the core of steppe armies such as those of the Mongol Empire, the Ilkhanate and the Khazar Khaganate, and of the Parthian Empire, famous for its horse archers. Foot archers were also important in earlier states, including the Akkadian and Kushite empires, the latter known for its bowmen.

The Ashkenazi Jews are Jewish communities originating in medieval Central Europe. Many settled in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which offered relative tolerance and legal privileges, and it became home to the largest Jewish population in the world. Their communal and religious life there shaped later Jewish history.

Athens is a city in Greece that was a leading city-state of the classical era. It was central to the resistance to the Achaemenid Empire during the Persian Wars, including the victory at Marathon in 490 BCE. After the closure of the Neoplatonist school in Athens in the sixth century, some of its philosophers took refuge at the court of the Sasanian king Khosrow I.

The Babylonian captivity was the period in the sixth century BCE when many inhabitants of the kingdom of Judah were deported to Babylonia by Nebuchadnezzar II of the Chaldean Empire, following the capture of Jerusalem. The exile ended after the Persian conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE, when Cyrus allowed the exiles to return. It strongly influenced the development of Judaism.

BASF is a German chemical company founded in 1865. It became one of the world's leading producers of synthetic dyes and later developed the industrial synthesis of ammonia. It was an example of the strength of the German Empire's chemical industry and science-based industrialisation.

The Battle of Ipsus was fought in 301 BCE in Phrygia between Antigonus I and his son Demetrius on one side and a coalition of Seleucus I, Lysimachus and Cassander on the other. Seleucus's war elephants were important in the fighting, and Antigonus was killed. The battle ended attempts to reunite Alexander's empire and secured the Seleucid Empire's hold on Syria.

The Battle of Lechfeld was fought in 955 CE near Augsburg, where Otto I of Saxony decisively defeated the invading Magyars. The victory ended the Magyar raids into the German lands and greatly enhanced Otto's prestige. It was followed by his coronation as emperor by Pope John XII in 962, the date most historians treat as the functional founding of the Holy Roman Empire.

The Battle of Pavia was fought in 1525 in northern Italy during the Italian Wars, between the forces of Charles V and the French army of Francis I. The imperial and Spanish army won a decisive victory and captured the French king. The battle confirmed Habsburg dominance in Italy and showed the firepower of Spanish arquebusiers, a basis of the Spanish Empire's military reputation.

The Battle of Raphia was fought in 217 BCE near Gaza during the Fourth Syrian War, between Ptolemy IV of Egypt and the Seleucid king Antiochus III. The Ptolemaic army won, with native Egyptian troops taking an important part. The battle encouraged the Ptolemaic Empire to recruit more Egyptians into its army, which in turn altered the balance of power within society.

The Battle of the Somme was fought from July to November 1916 in northern France during the First World War, between British and French forces and the army of the German Empire. It was one of the bloodiest battles in history, with enormous losses on both sides and little ground changing hands. The battle was an example of the attritional warfare that steadily wore down German military strength.

Bayer is a German chemical and pharmaceutical company founded in the nineteenth century. Along with BASF and Hoechst, it led the chemical industry of the German Empire, which by 1913 dominated the global market for synthetic dyes. The company is an example of the science-based industrial growth that made Germany the largest economy in continental Europe.

Bishapur was a city in southwestern Iran founded by the Sasanian king Shapur I in the third century CE. Its construction drew on the labour and engineering skills of Roman prisoners captured in Shapur's campaigns. The city shows the Sasanian Empire's deliberate use of captured expertise in building and infrastructure.

Bithynia is a historical region in northwestern Anatolia, bordering the Sea of Marmara and the Black Sea. In the late thirteenth century its Byzantine borderlands near Bursa were the home of the beylik of Osman I. The region's position on the frontier between the Islamic and Byzantine worlds attracted ghazi warriors and made it the place where the Ottoman Empire began.

The Cape Colony was the settlement at the Cape of Good Hope established in 1652 by the Dutch East India Company as a resupply station for ships sailing to Asia. It grew into a settler colony whose descendants formed the Afrikaner community. The colony outlasted the rule of the Dutch Empire there and passed to Britain in the early nineteenth century.

The capture of Malacca in 1641 was the conquest of the Portuguese-held port on the Strait of Malacca by the Dutch East India Company and its Johor allies. It was an example of the Dutch strategy of seizing chokepoints of maritime trade rather than large territories. The victory consolidated the Dutch Empire's dominance over Southeast Asian sea routes.

The Carolingian Empire was the Frankish realm ruled by the Carolingian dynasty, reaching its height under Charlemagne, who was crowned emperor in Rome in 800. It covered much of western and central Europe and encouraged the Carolingian Renaissance. Divided by the Treaty of Verdun in 843, it was the forerunner of France and of the Holy Roman Empire, and exchanged embassies with the Abbasid Caliphate.

A chariot is a light, two-wheeled, horse-drawn vehicle used in warfare, carrying a driver and an archer or spearman. Chariots were decisive weapons in the Late Bronze Age, used by the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom, the Hittite Empire and the Mitanni Empire, known for their horse training. They remained in use by the Assyrian Empire and in early Indian warfare, including the Maurya army.

The chonin were the townspeople of Edo-period Japan, mainly merchants and artisans. Confucian theory placed them below the samurai and the peasants, though historians now hold that in law the commoners were classed, not ranked, beneath the samurai. They grew wealthy through commerce in cities such as Edo and Osaka. Their prosperity sustained an urban culture that included kabuki and woodblock prints.

The Congress of Vienna was a conference of European powers held in 1814–1815 to reorganise Europe after the Napoleonic Wars. Alexander I was a dominant figure there, establishing the Russian Empire as one of the five great powers. The congress also partially restored the Dutch Empire, while confirming Britain's retention of the Cape and Ceylon.

Cyril and Methodius were Byzantine Greek brothers and missionaries of the ninth century who worked among the Slavs of central Europe. They created the Glagolitic alphabet and translated liturgical texts into Old Church Slavonic. Their work was the basis of Slavic Christian literature and spread the Byzantine Empire's cultural influence.

The da'wa ('summons' or 'mission') was the missionary and propaganda organisation of Ismaili Islam. Under the Fatimid Caliphate it was a hierarchical institution that spread Ismaili doctrine and loyalty to the imam-caliph across the Islamic world, and it was central to the dynasty's rise in North Africa and to its governance. Divisions within the movement later contributed to the caliphate's weakening.

Dawit I was an emperor of Ethiopia in the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. His campaigns against the Muslim Ifat Sultanate led to the capture and execution of its ruler Sa'ad ad-Din II around 1410. This defeat drove the surviving Walashma princes across the Gulf of Aden and led to the founding of the Adal Sultanate.

The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was a chartered trading company founded in 1602, with powers to wage war, make treaties and govern territory in Asia. It was the main instrument of the Dutch Empire in the East Indies, displaced the Portuguese Empire from much of the spice trade and was a model and rival for the English East India Company of the British Empire.

The Dutch West India Company was a chartered company established in 1621 to conduct Dutch trade and warfare in the Atlantic. It was central to the Dutch Empire's activities in West Africa, Brazil, the Caribbean and North America, including the Atlantic slave trade, though it struggled financially and was later reorganised.

The Eagle and Jaguar warriors were elite military orders of the Aztec Empire. Membership was earned mainly by capturing enemies in battle, and it brought high status, distinctive costumes and privileges. These orders show the close link between warfare, religion and social advancement in Aztec society.

The fall of Constantinople was the capture of the Byzantine capital by the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II in 1453, after a siege in which heavy artillery had a large part. It ended the Byzantine Empire and made the city the Ottoman capital. The Ottoman recovery that made it possible followed the empire's defeat by Timur in 1402, a link noted in the Timurid Empire profile.

Fancheng was a city on the Han River in central China, paired with Xiangyang on the opposite bank. Together the twin cities guarded the route to the Yangtze valley, and they resisted the Mongol siege of 1267–1273; their fall opened the way to the conquest of the Southern Song Dynasty.

Fin de siècle ('end of the century') refers to the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, a period associated with cultural innovation and a sense of decadence. In Vienna, the capital of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, it saw a flowering in psychoanalysis, philosophy, painting, architecture and music.

The First Chimurenga was the uprising of the Ndebele and Shona against the British South Africa Company in 1896–1897, in what is now Zimbabwe. Religious networks, notably the Mwari cult it had patronised, helped to organise Shona resistance.

Françafrique is a term for the close and often informal political, economic and military ties that France maintained with its former African colonies after independence. It reflects the continued influence of the French Empire, including the role of French-educated elites in post-independence leadership.

Gustav Klimt was an Austrian painter and a leading figure of the Vienna Secession, known for decorative works such as The Kiss. He was one of the central artists of Vienna's cultural flowering around 1900. The site presents him as part of the artistic and intellectual life of the Austro-Hungarian Empire in its final decades.

The Han River is a major tributary of the Yangtze in central China. The twin cities of Xiangyang and Fancheng on its banks guarded the approach to the Yangtze valley. Their long siege by Mongol forces between 1267 and 1273 was a turning point in the fall of the Song Dynasty.

The Henrician Articles were a set of constitutional principles adopted in 1573 and sworn by each newly elected king of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, named after the first elected king, Henry of Valois. They guaranteed free royal election, regular sessions of the Sejm, religious toleration and the nobility's right to resist a king who broke them. They were central to the Commonwealth's governance.

The Hijra was the migration of the Prophet Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, which marks the start of the Islamic calendar. In Medina the first Muslim community-state was formed, the basis of the later Rashidun Caliphate. It was also a model for later movements, notably Usman dan Fodio's migration in the foundation of the Sokoto Caliphate.

Hoechst was a German chemical and pharmaceutical company founded in the nineteenth century. Together with BASF and Bayer, it led the German chemical industry, which dominated world synthetic dye production before the First World War. It is an example of the industrial strength of the German Empire.

Horse breeding is the raising of horses for transport, warfare and trade. It underpinned the military power of many empires. The Mitanni Empire was known for chariot horses, the Gokturk Empire and Khazar Khaganate depended on steppe herds, and the Oyo Empire maintained horses for its cavalry.

Huo Qubing was a Han Dynasty general of the second century BCE, known for his cavalry campaigns against the Xiongnu under Emperor Wu. His deep raids into the steppe inflicted major defeats and helped secure the Hexi Corridor. He died young but is remembered as one of the most brilliant commanders against the Xiongnu Empire.

Ife is an ancient city in south-western Nigeria, regarded as the spiritual birthplace of the Yoruba people and known for its bronze and terracotta sculpture. Benin traditions link the founding of the Oba dynasty to a prince from Ife. This connection is part of the foundation history of the Benin Empire.

The Igun Eronmwon were the royal guild of bronze casters in the Benin kingdom, working under the patronage of the Oba. They produced the cast brass and bronze works known as the Benin Bronzes. Their street in Benin City still continues the tradition, which survives from the Benin Empire.

Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman whose victory in civil war made him dictator, before his assassination in 44 BCE. His intervention in Egypt supported Cleopatra VII, and their relationship drew the Ptolemaic Empire into Roman politics. His career led to the foundation of the Roman Empire under Augustus.

The Koutoubia Mosque is the principal mosque of Marrakesh, built under the Almohad Caliphate in the twelfth century. Its minaret is one of the finest examples of Almohad architecture and influenced later towers such as the Giralda of Seville and the Hassan Tower in Rabat. It remains a landmark of the city and a surviving monument of Almohad rule.

Kufa was a garrison city founded by Arab Muslim forces in southern Iraq in the 630s during the Rashidun conquests. It became a major political and religious centre and served as the capital of the caliph Ali. Its population was central to the conflicts that ended the Rashidun Caliphate, and it remained a centre of Alid sympathy.

Leather is animal hide tanned and prepared for making goods such as bags, sandals, saddles and book covers. The Hausa cities of the Sokoto Caliphate, particularly Kano, were known for fine dyed leather. According to the Sokoto profile, leather goods were among the principal commodities of the caliphate's long-distance trade.

Li Hongzhang was a leading Chinese statesman and general of the late Qing Empire. He had a large part in suppressing the Taiping Rebellion and promoted the Self-Strengthening Movement, building arsenals, industries and a modern navy. He negotiated several treaties after Qing defeats, including the Treaty of Shimonoseki with Japan in 1895.

Ludwig Wittgenstein was a philosopher born in Vienna in 1889 into one of the wealthiest families of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. He became one of the most influential philosophers of the twentieth century, working mainly in Cambridge. He is often cited as part of the intellectual culture of late Habsburg Vienna.

The Maluku Islands, or Moluccas, are an archipelago in eastern Indonesia, historically known as the Spice Islands. They were the original source of cloves, nutmeg and mace, which were highly prized in global trade. The Dutch East India Company seized control of the spice trade there in the seventeenth century, making it central to the Dutch Empire's economy.

Mount Ararat is a high volcanic mountain in eastern Anatolia, near the borders of present-day Turkey, Armenia and Iran. The surrounding region had a large Armenian population. Shah Abbas I of the Safavid Empire relocated Armenian merchant communities from the Ararat region to New Julfa in Isfahan, where they took a leading part in the silk trade.

Mursili I was an early king of the Hittites, remembered for his long-distance raid down the Euphrates around 1595 BCE. The campaign sacked Babylon, carried off the statues of Marduk and his consort, and ended the First Babylonian Dynasty. For the Hittite Empire it demonstrated a long operational reach, though it produced no lasting territorial gain, while for the Babylonian Empire it marked the final blow to the Old Babylonian state.

Nahuatl is a Uto-Aztecan language spoken by the Mexica and other peoples of central Mexico. The Aztec Empire spread its use across Mesoamerica, and it carried a tradition of poetry and learning. After the Spanish conquest it became the most important indigenous lingua franca of the colonial period, used by missionaries for evangelisation.

Naqsh-e Jahan Square is a large public square in Isfahan, Iran, laid out under Shah Abbas I when he made the city the Safavid capital. It is framed by major monuments including royal mosques and the Ali Qapu palace. It is among the best-known architectural achievements of the Safavid Empire.

The Navigation Acts were a series of English laws from the mid-seventeenth century that restricted colonial trade to English ships and English ports. Aimed in large part at Dutch commercial dominance, they were central to English mercantilism. They helped build the shipping, trade and fiscal base on which the early British Empire grew.

Nezahualcoyotl was a ruler of the city-state of Texcoco in the fifteenth century, also known as a poet and builder. As an exiled prince he joined the Mexica leader Itzcoatl and the city of Tlacopan in a coalition against Azcapotzalco. Their victory created the Triple Alliance that formed the basis of the Aztec Empire.

Northern Europe is the region comprising Scandinavia, the Baltic lands and neighbouring areas. In the early medieval period it was connected to the Islamic world by trade routes running along the Volga. The Khazar Khaganate helped channel silver dirhams northwards, which became a basis of Viking commerce.

The Numidians were Berber peoples of the North African interior west of Carthage, in present-day Algeria and Tunisia. They were known for their light cavalry and formed an important part of the Punic Empire's armies. Numidian rulers later allied with Rome, and their cavalry contributed to Carthage's defeat at Zama.

The Order of Assassins is the popular name for the Nizari Ismailis of Iran and Syria in the medieval period, founded under Hasan-i Sabbah in the Alborz mountains. Arising from the Fatimid succession crisis of 1094, they were known for targeted killings of political opponents. Their name gave rise to the English word assassin, and their lineage, which goes back to the Fatimid Caliphate, continues through the Aga Khan.

The Organisation of African Unity was an intergovernmental body of independent African states founded in Addis Ababa in 1963. Emperor Haile Selassie took a leading part in its creation. Its establishment confirmed Ethiopia's role as a diplomatic centre of African independence, an important legacy of the Ethiopian Empire, and it was replaced by the African Union in 2002.

Papinian was a Roman jurist of the late second and early third centuries CE, regarded as one of the greatest legal minds of the classical period. Alongside Gaius, Ulpian and Paulus he helped develop a sophisticated body of Roman law. Their writings were later preserved in Justinian's Digest and remain part of the legacy of the Roman Empire.

The Persepolis Fortification Tablets are a large archive of clay administrative tablets from the reign of Darius I, found at Persepolis. Most are written in Elamite and record the distribution of food and supplies to workers and officials. They show how Elamite administrative language and practice were absorbed into the Achaemenid state, an inheritance from the Elamite Confederation.

Persia is the historical name for Iran, derived from the region of Pars in the south-west. It was the heartland of the Achaemenid, Parthian and Sasanian empires and later of the Safavid, Afsharid and Zand dynasties. Conquered by the Macedonian Empire, the Umayyad Caliphate and the Mongols, it also exerted a strong cultural influence on its conquerors, from the Abbasid Caliphate to the Timurid Empire.

Philip II was king of Macedon from 359 to 336 BCE and the father of Alexander the Great. He professionalised the Macedonian army, introduced the sarissa phalanx and used diplomacy and conquest to dominate the Greek city-states. His reforms made the Macedonian Empire possible, and he was assassinated in 336 BCE.

The Processional Way was a monumental street in Babylon leading through the Ishtar Gate, decorated with glazed brick reliefs of lions. It was used for religious processions, especially during the New Year festival. Built under Nebuchadnezzar II, it is an example of the Chaldean Empire's investment in monumental architecture.

Puzur-Ashur I was an early ruler of the city of Assur in northern Mesopotamia, around the twentieth century BCE. He founded a dynasty that gave Assyrian history continuity. In this early period Assur's power rested on its commercial network of merchant colonies in Anatolia, the foundation of the later Assyrian Empire.

The Qutb Minar is a tall minaret of red sandstone in Delhi, begun around the end of the twelfth century under Qutb ud-Din Aibak and completed by his successors. It stands within a complex that includes one of the earliest mosques in India. It is an example of the Indo-Islamic architectural synthesis of the Delhi Sultanate.

The rule of law is the principle that all people and institutions, including governments, are subject to and accountable under publicly known laws applied equally. It is closely associated with British constitutional traditions. Accounts of the British Empire note the paradox that the liberal values the empire claimed to stand for, including the rule of law, gave colonial subjects ideological weapons to challenge imperial rule.

The Sankore Madrasah was an Islamic centre of learning based around the Sankore Mosque in Timbuktu. Together with other mosques and scholarly households in the city it formed a widely known network of teaching in theology, law, astronomy and other subjects. Accounts of the Songhai Empire present it as a symbol of Timbuktu's flourishing scholarly culture under Songhai rule.

The Scythians were a group of Iranian-speaking nomadic peoples who dominated the Eurasian steppe north of the Black Sea and beyond in the first millennium BCE. Known as mounted archers, they interacted with and raided the settled empires of the Near East. They dominated Media for a time according to the Median Empire profile, and the Achaemenid ruler Darius I campaigned against them around 513 BCE.

A secret society is an organisation whose membership, rituals or knowledge are restricted to initiates. In the Luba Empire the Bambudye society acted as custodian of historical memory and as a check on royal excess. The Luba Empire and Lunda Empire profiles both show such societies taking an important part in governance and political legitimacy.

Sennacherib was king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 705 to 681 BCE, known for rebuilding Nineveh as a capital. He fought repeated wars against Babylon and Elam and destroyed Babylon in 689 BCE. His harsh treatment of Babylon fed lasting resentment, and he was assassinated by his own sons.

The Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque is a mosque on the eastern side of the Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan, built under Shah Abbas I in the early seventeenth century. It is known for the tilework of its dome and interior. Accounts of the Safavid Empire cite it as part of Isfahan's architectural ensemble.

Shi'ism is the branch of Islam that holds that leadership of the community belongs to the descendants of Ali ibn Abi Talib. Its Ismaili form was the faith of the Fatimid Caliphate, whose decline ended Ismaili rule in Egypt. Accounts of the Ilkhanate note Shi'ism's influence on religion in Persia after the Ilkhanid ruler Öljeitü converted to it.

The Siege of Jerusalem in 587 BCE was the capture and destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldean (Neo-Babylonian) king Nebuchadnezzar II. The Temple was destroyed and much of the population was deported to Babylon. Accounts of the Chaldean Empire note that this exile shaped later Jewish history.

The Siege of Xiangyang was a long siege of the twin cities of Xiangyang and Fancheng on the Han River from 1267 to 1273. Mongol forces of the Yuan Dynasty eventually took them using counterweight trebuchets. Accounts of the Song Dynasty treat the fall of Xiangyang as the event that opened the Yangtze to the Mongol conquest of the Southern Song.

Siege warfare is the conduct of military operations to capture or defend fortified places, through blockade, assault, mining or bombardment. The Assyrian Empire was known for its siege engineering, and the Babylonian, Chaldean, Hittite and Macedonian empires also relied on it. Later the Ottoman Empire's artillery made it a master of siege warfare.

Sigmund Freud was an Austrian neurologist who founded psychoanalysis, working in Vienna from the late nineteenth century. His theories of the unconscious mind strongly influenced psychology and culture. Accounts of the Austro-Hungarian Empire name him among the figures of Vienna's fin-de-siècle intellectual flowering.

The Song Dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279, first from Kaifeng in the north and then, after the Jin conquest of the north, from Hangzhou in the south. It saw economic growth, urbanisation, paper money, printing and gunpowder weapons, along with a civil service recruited by examination. It was conquered by the Mongols, who founded the Yuan Dynasty.

A spirit medium is a person believed to be possessed by and speak for ancestral or other spirits. In the Mutapa Empire spirit mediums interpreted the will of the ancestors and influenced political decisions. Accounts of the Mutapa Empire describe them as important in governance.

Syncretism is the blending of different religious, philosophical or cultural traditions into new combined forms. The Macedonian Empire's conquests encouraged a fusion of Greek and Eastern knowledge, while the Roman Empire absorbed foreign deities into its pantheon. In the Songhai Empire, the term describes Sunni Ali's mixture of Islam with indigenous religious practice, which his successor Askia Muhammad replaced with a more orthodox Islamic legitimacy.

The Tang Code was the comprehensive penal code of the Tang Dynasty, issued with an official commentary, the Tang Lü Shuyi, in 653. It defined crimes and punishments systematically and reflected Confucian principles of hierarchy and family relationships. Accounts of the Tang Dynasty treat it as central to Tang governance, and it was a model for later Chinese dynasties and for legal codes in Japan, Korea and Vietnam.

The Targowica Confederation was an alliance of Polish-Lithuanian magnates formed in 1792 to overturn the reformist Constitution of 3 May 1791. Backed by Catherine the Great, it invited Russian military intervention. Accounts of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth describe it as a confederation of nobles who preferred foreign domination to the loss of their privileges, leading to the Second Partition of 1793.

Tawhid is the Islamic doctrine of the absolute oneness and unity of God, a central principle of Islamic theology. The reformer Ibn Tumart placed an uncompromising interpretation of tawhid at the centre of his teaching. His followers called themselves al-Muwahhidun, the upholders of divine unity, from which the name of the Almohad Caliphate derives.

Taxila was an ancient city in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent, in present-day Pakistan, known as a centre of trade and learning. It lay on routes connecting India with Central Asia and Iran. Accounts of the Maurya Empire name it, alongside Pataliputra and Ujjain, as one of the urban centres that contributed to craft production, coinage and long-distance commerce.

The tercio was a Spanish infantry formation of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries that combined pikemen, swordsmen and arquebusiers in large, disciplined squares. It made the armies of the Spanish Empire among the strongest in Europe. Accounts of the Swedish Empire note that Gustavus Adolphus reformed this model by breaking the tercio's massive squares into smaller, more manoeuvrable brigades of musketeers and pikemen.

Texcoco was a major city-state on the eastern shore of Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico and one of the three members of the Aztec Triple Alliance. Known as a centre of law, poetry and learning, especially under its ruler Nezahualcoyotl, it received two-fifths of the alliance's tribute revenues. Factions of the Texcocans sided with the Spanish during the conquest.

Tibetan Buddhism is the form of Buddhism that developed in Tibet, combining Mahayana and Vajrayana teachings with distinctive monastic institutions. Under the Yuan Dynasty, Tibetan lamas received special privileges from Kublai Khan onward. Accounts of the Yuan Dynasty describe this period as decisive in the spread of Tibetan Buddhism into Mongolia and notes the Phagspa script created by the Tibetan lama Phagpa.

Tinmel is a village in the High Atlas Mountains of Morocco. In the early twelfth century the religious reformer Ibn Tumart established his base there after proclaiming himself the Mahdi, making it the place where the Almohad movement began. Its twelfth-century mosque, built under the Almohads, survives as an important monument.

The Treaty of Zuhab was the peace agreement of 1639 between the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire. It ended a long series of wars and left Iraq and Baghdad in Ottoman hands. Accounts of the Safavid Empire note that the frontier it established approximates the modern border between Iran and Iraq.

The triangular trade was the Atlantic commercial system linking Europe, West Africa and the Americas from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries. Manufactured goods went from Europe to Africa, enslaved Africans were transported to the Americas, and plantation products such as sugar returned to Europe. Accounts of the Oyo Empire describe Oyo as an indispensable structural node in this commerce through its central place in the Atlantic slave trade.

Tukulti-Ninurta I was a king of Assyria in the thirteenth century BCE, one of the most powerful rulers of the Middle Assyrian period. Accounts of the Assyrian Empire emphasise his conquest of Babylon around 1225 BCE and his personal capture of the Kassite king. He also founded a new royal city, Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta, near Assur.

The Turkic peoples are a large family of ethnic groups speaking Turkic languages, originating in the steppes of Inner and Central Asia. The Gokturk Empire was the first state to bear the Turkic name, and Turkic groups later founded or dominated the Seljuk Empire, the Ottoman Empire, the Khazar Khaganate and the Delhi Sultanate. As soldiers and slave-soldiers they were also central to the Abbasid Caliphate and the Mamluk Sultanate.

Ulugh Beg was a Timurid ruler and astronomer, a grandson of Timur, who governed Samarkand for decades and died in 1449. He built a great observatory and madrasa in Samarkand and sponsored astronomical tables of great accuracy. His brief reign as supreme ruler ended with his overthrow and death at the instigation of his son.

Venice is a city in north-eastern Italy built on islands in a lagoon, which became a major maritime and commercial republic in the medieval period. Venetian merchants gained extensive trading privileges in the Byzantine Empire from 1082, and Venice took a leading part in the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople in 1204. It long dominated Europe's trade in Asian luxuries until the Portuguese opened the sea route to India.

The Vienna Secession was an art movement founded in 1897 by Gustav Klimt and other artists who broke away from Vienna's established academic art association. It promoted modern styles in painting, architecture and design. Accounts of the Austro-Hungarian Empire place it within the cultural flowering of late imperial Vienna.

The Vikings were seafaring Scandinavians who raided, traded and settled across Europe from the late eighth to the eleventh centuries. Their raids devastated the coasts and river valleys of the divided Carolingian kingdoms, and accounts of the Carolingian Empire note Charles the Fat's payment of tribute to the Vikings besieging Paris. Accounts of the Khazar Khaganate note that Khazar trade helped spread silver dirhams into Northern Europe, a basis of Viking commerce.

Xiangyang is a city on the Han River in central China, which with its twin city Fancheng formed the gateway to the Yangtze valley. The Mongol siege of Xiangyang from 1267 to 1273 was the decisive confrontation in the conquest of the Southern Song. The city fell only after counterweight trebuchets built by Persian engineers were deployed, opening the way for the Yuan conquest of southern China.

The Xiongnu Empire was a confederation of nomadic peoples that dominated the eastern Eurasian steppe from the late third century BCE to the first century CE. Under the chanyu Modu it united the steppe tribes and became a strong rival of the Han Dynasty, extracting tribute through the heqin system. Weakened by Han campaigns and internal division, it fragmented, though its political model influenced later steppe empires.

Xoconusco, or Soconusco, is a region on the Pacific coast of southern Mexico, in modern Chiapas, known for its cacao. The ruler Ahuitzotl extended the empire south to Xoconusco and into what is now Guatemala. It became one of the most distant and valuable tributary provinces of the empire.
